pieces.text: Read the following passage from

content.text: The Great Gatsby

pieces.text: . In this excerpt, Nick Carraway, the narrator, receives a visit from his next-door neighbor, Jay Gatsby. Gatsby has a romantic interest in Nick's cousin, Daisy Buchanan. Nick learned about Gatsby's interest earlier that night from Daisy's friend Jordan Baker. In that conversation, Jordan made it clear that Gatsby would like Nick to arrange for a meeting between Gatsby and Daisy.

textContent.text: When I came home to West Egg that night I was afraid for a moment that my house was on fire. Two o'clock and the whole corner of the peninsula was blazing with light, which fell unreal on the shrubbery and made thin elongating glints upon the roadside wires. Turning a corner, I saw that it was Gatsby's house, lit from tower to cellar.

At first I thought it was another party, a wild rout that had resolved itself into "hide-and-go-seek" or "sardines-in-the-box" with all the house thrown open to the game. But there wasn't a sound. Only wind in the trees, which blew the wires and made the lights go off and on again as if the house had winked into the darkness. As my taxi groaned away I saw Gatsby walking toward me across his lawn.
"Your place looks like the World's Fair," I said.
"Does it?" He turned his eyes toward it absently. "I have been glancing into some of the rooms. Let's go to Coney Island, old sport. In my car."
"It's too late."
"Well, suppose we take a plunge in the swimming pool? I haven't made use of it all summer."
"I've got to go to bed."
"All right."
He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.
"I talked with Miss Baker," I said after a moment. "I'm going to call up Daisy tomorrow and invite her over here to tea."
"Oh, that's all right," he said carelessly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble."
"What day would suit you?"

pieces.text: "What day would suit

content.text: you

pieces.text: ?" he corrected me quickly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble, you see."

textContent.text: "How about the day after tomorrow?"
He considered for a moment. Then, with reluctance: "I want to get the grass cut," he said.
We both looked down at the grass—there was a sharp line where my ragged lawn ended and the darker, well-kept expanse of his began. I suspected that he meant my grass.
"There's another little thing," he said uncertainly, and hesitated.
"Would you rather put it off for a few days?" I asked.
"Oh, it isn't about that. At least—" He fumbled with a series of beginnings.
"Why, I thought—why, look here, old sport, you don't make much money, do you?"
"Not very much."
This seemed to reassure him and he continued more confidently.

"I thought you didn't, if you'll pardon my—you see, I carry on a little business on the side, a sort of side line, you understand. And I thought that if you don't make very much—You're selling bonds, aren't you, old sport?"
"Trying to."
"Well, this would interest you. It wouldn't take up much of your time and you might pick up a nice bit of money. It happens to be a rather confidential sort of thing."

I realize now that under different circumstances that conversation might have been one of the crises of my life. But, because the offer was obviously and tactlessly for a service to be rendered, I had no choice except to cut him off there.
"I've got my hands full," I said. "I'm much obliged but I couldn't take on any more work."
He waited a moment longer, hoping I'd begin a conversation, but I was too absorbed to be responsive, so he went unwillingly home.
<citation>Adapted from F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby</citation>

content.text: Great Inspiration

alternativeText.text: Movie poster for the first film adaptation of The Great Gatsby.

pieces.text: Great novels often inspire adaptations in other media, and

content.text: The Great Gatsby

pieces.text: is no exception.

content.text: The book
has inspired several acclaimed young adult novels, a ballet, and even a Taylor Swift song called "Happiness."
Hollywood studios have adapted the novel for film at least six times.

pieces.text: The first movie version of

content.text: The Great Gatsby

pieces.text: screened just a year after the book's publication, at a time when film was still a relatively new medium. It is unknown exactly how the 1926 version went about telling Gatsby's story, as no known copies of that movie exist; it is among the seventy-eight percent of American feature films from the silent era that have been lost to decomposition and neglect.

contents.text: The details in this passage support this inference about Gatsby's internal conflict:

text.text: His desire to appear casually aloof conflicts with his feelings of excitement for Daisy's visit.

contents.text: These inferences about Gatsby are not supported by the passage:

text.text: His romantic interest in Daisy conflicts with his eagerness to have Nick come to work for him.

content.text: Gatsby does not seem to see a conflict between his interest in Daisy and his interest in keeping Nick close to him.

text.text: His hope that Nick will invite Daisy over conflicts with his fear that Daisy will not remember him.

content.text: Gatsby does not express fear that Daisy has forgotten him.

text.text: His desire for Nick's assistance conflicts with his fundamental disdain for people with Nick's low social standing.

content.text: While it is true that Nick is considerably less wealthy than Gatsby, Gatsby does not act with disdain or intentional disrespect toward his neighbor. If anything,
Gatsby seems deferential to Nick when he says that he doesn't want to put him to any trouble.

contents.text: The details in these quotes suggest that Gatsby is trying to appear casually aloof:

text.text: He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.

content.text: Nick senses that Gatsby wants to talk about Daisy's potential visit but that he is suppressing, or holding back, his desire to broach the subject. A likely explanation for Gatsby's hesitation is that he is trying to project an aura of relaxed confidence.

text.text: "Oh, that's all right," he said carelessly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble."

content.text: Gatsby tries to project a tone of casual indifference about the details surrounding Daisy's visit. While his excessive politeness and his fretting about the lawn suggest that he is actually quite nervous and tense, he seems to want Nick to think that he is very cool and relaxed.

contents.text: The details in this passage suggest that this is why Nick brushes aside Gatsby's job offer:

text.text: Nick is not comfortable accepting a favor in exchange for helping Gatsby.

content.text: Nick says that Gatsby's job offer is obviously in exchange for a service and, as such, he "has no choice" but to reject it. This indicates that Nick does not feel comfortable trading on his connection with Daisy for profit.

contents.text: These inferences are not supported by the passage:

text.text: Nick does not approve of Gatsby's business and can't imagine working with him.

content.text: Nick says that under other circumstances, he would have considered Gatsby's offer seriously. He rejects it because he thinks the offer itself is crass and tactless, not because he disapproves of Gatsby's business practices.

text.text: Nick is offended that Gatsby makes assumptions about Nick's job and finances.

content.text: Nick seems to humbly agree that he doesn't make very much money as a bond salesman. He doesn't seem offended by Gatsby's assumptions.

text.text: Nick's job is keeping him so busy that he doesn't have time to work for Gatsby.

content.text: Nick suggests that he could have been tempted to accept Gatsby's offer if it didn't come with such obvious strings attached. Though he says he can't take on more work, it seems that Nick is using his job as an excuse to reject Gatsby's offer, which he sees as unscrupulous under the circumstances.

Turning a corner, I saw that it was Gatsby's house, lit from tower to cellar.

At first I thought it was another party, a wild rout that had resolved itself into "hide-and-go-seek" or "sardines-in-the-box" with all the house thrown open to the game. But there wasn't a sound. Only wind in the trees, which blew the wires and made the lights go off and on again as if the house had winked into the darkness. As my taxi groaned away I saw Gatsby walking toward me across his lawn.
"Your place looks like the World's Fair," I said.
"Does it?" He turned his eyes toward it absently. "I have been glancing into some of the rooms. Let's go to Coney Island, old sport. In my car."
"It's too late."
"Well, suppose we take a plunge in the swimming pool? I haven't made use of it all summer."
"I've got to go to bed."
"All right."
He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.
"I talked with Miss Baker," I said after a moment. "I'm going to call up Daisy tomorrow and invite her over here to tea."
"Oh, that's all right," he said carelessly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble."
"What day would suit you?"

content.text: He considered for a moment. Then, with reluctance: "I want to get the grass cut," he said.

textContent.text: We both looked down at the grass—there was a sharp line where my ragged lawn ended and the darker, well-kept expanse of his began. I suspected that he meant my grass.
"There's another little thing," he said uncertainly, and hesitated.
"Would you rather put it off for a few days?" I asked.
"Oh, it isn't about that. At least—" He fumbled with a series of beginnings.
"Why, I thought—why, look here, old sport, you don't make much money, do you?"
"Not very much."
This seemed to reassure him and he continued more confidently.

"I thought you didn't, if you'll pardon my—you see, I carry on a little business on the side, a sort of side line, you understand. And I thought that if you don't make very much—You're selling bonds, aren't you, old sport?"
"Trying to."
"Well, this would interest you. It wouldn't take up much of your time and you might pick up a nice bit of money. It happens to be a rather confidential sort of thing."

I realize now that under different circumstances that conversation might have been one of the crises of my life. But, because the offer was obviously and tactlessly for a service to be rendered, I had no choice except to cut him off there.
"I've got my hands full," I said. "I'm much obliged but I couldn't take on any more work."
He waited a moment longer, hoping I'd begin a conversation, but I was too absorbed to be responsive, so he went unwillingly home.
<citation>Adapted from F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby</citation>

text.text: He wants to be sure that Daisy will be impressed when she visits.

text.text: He wants to signal his disapproval to Nick regarding the state of Nick's property.

content.text: The appearance of the lawn doesn't seem to concern Gatsby except within the context of Daisy's visit. There is no evidence in the passage to suggest that Gatsby disapproves of the way Nick maintains his property, or that he is trying to signal disapproval to Nick.

content.text: The passage does not mention damage to the lawn from a party.

text.text: He wants to thank Nick for setting up Daisy's visit by offering him free lawn care.

content.text: Gatsby does mention wanting to have the grass cut, but he seems motivated by a desire to impress Daisy, rather than a desire to show gratitude to Nick.

contents.text: Immediately after Nick confirms his willingness to help Gatsby by arranging a meeting with Daisy, Gatsby abruptly changes the subject by offering Nick a job. Gatsby's offer of "a nice bit of money" for little effort is tempting to Nick, but Nick sees it as repayment for a favor, which he finds objectionable. This evidence suggests that the most likely reason that Gatsby offers Nick a job is as repayment for arranging a meeting with Daisy.

pieces.text: Great novels often inspire adaptations in other media, and

content.text: The Great Gatsby

pieces.text: is no exception.

content.text: The book
has inspired several acclaimed young adult novels, a ballet, and even a Taylor Swift song called "Happiness."
Hollywood studios have adapted the novel for film at least six times.

pieces.text: The first movie version of

content.text: The Great Gatsby

pieces.text: screened just a year after the book's publication, at a time when film was still a relatively new medium. It is unknown exactly how the 1926 version went about telling Gatsby's story, as no known copies of that movie exist; it is among the seventy-eight percent of American feature films from the silent era that have been lost to decomposition and neglect.

text.text: He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.

content.text: Nick senses that Gatsby wants to talk about Daisy's potential visit but that he is suppressing, or holding back, his desire to broach the subject. A likely explanation for Gatsby's hesitation is that he is trying to project an aura of relaxed confidence.

text.text: "Oh, that's all right," he said carelessly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble."

content.text: Gatsby tries to project a tone of casual indifference about the details surrounding Daisy's visit. While his excessive politeness and his fretting about the lawn suggest that he is actually quite nervous and tense, he seems to want Nick to think that he is very cool and relaxed.

contents.text: The details in this passage suggest that this is why Nick brushes aside Gatsby's job offer:

text.text: Nick is not comfortable accepting a favor in exchange for helping Gatsby.

content.text: Nick says that Gatsby's job offer is obviously in exchange for a service and, as such, he "has no choice" but to reject it. This indicates that Nick does not feel comfortable trading on his connection with Daisy for profit.

contents.text: These inferences are not supported by the passage:

text.text: Nick does not approve of Gatsby's business and can't imagine working with him.

content.text: Nick says that under other circumstances, he would have considered Gatsby's offer seriously. He rejects it because he thinks the offer itself is crass and tactless, not because he disapproves of Gatsby's business practices.

text.text: Nick is offended that Gatsby makes assumptions about Nick's job and finances.

content.text: Nick seems to humbly agree that he doesn't make very much money as a bond salesman. He doesn't seem offended by Gatsby's assumptions.

text.text: Nick's job is keeping him so busy that he doesn't have time to work for Gatsby.

content.text: Nick suggests that he could have been tempted to accept Gatsby's offer if it didn't come with such obvious strings attached. Though he says he can't take on more work, it seems that Nick is using his job as an excuse to reject Gatsby's offer, which he sees as unscrupulous under the circumstances.

text.text: He is desperate to win Nick's friendship.

content.text: Gatsby offers to take Nick to Coney Island, and he asks Nick to go swimming with him, but he does not seem particularly upset when Nick declines these offers.

text.text: He is quietly competitive with Nick about money.

content.text: Gatsby seems uncomfortable throughout this passage. The one thing that seems to offer him some sense of confidence is his wealth relative to Nick's. This suggests that he does not see Nick as a financial competitor.

text.text: He is insincere in his offers to entertain Nick.

content.text: Though he likely has ulterior motives, nothing in the text suggests that Gatsby is being insincere when he invites Nick to Coney Island and to his swimming pool.

Two o'clock and the whole corner of the peninsula was blazing with light, which fell unreal on the shrubbery and made thin elongating glints upon the roadside wires. Turning a corner, I saw that it was Gatsby's house, lit from tower to cellar.

At first I thought it was another party, a wild rout that had resolved itself into "hide-and-go-seek" or "sardines-in-the-box" with all the house thrown open to the game. But there wasn't a sound. Only wind in the trees, which blew the wires and made the lights go off and on again as if the house had winked into the darkness. As my taxi groaned away I saw Gatsby walking toward me across his lawn.
"Your place looks like the World's Fair," I said.
"Does it?" He turned his eyes toward it absently. "I have been glancing into some of the rooms. Let's go to Coney Island, old sport. In my car."
"It's too late."
"Well, suppose we take a plunge in the swimming pool? I haven't made use of it all summer."
"I've got to go to bed."
"All right."
He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.
"I talked with Miss Baker," I said after a moment. "I'm going to call up Daisy tomorrow and invite her over here to tea."
"Oh, that's all right," he said carelessly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble."
"What day would suit you?"

content.text: you

pieces.text: ?" he corrected me quickly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble, you see."

textContent.text: "How about the day after tomorrow?"
He considered for a moment. Then, with reluctance: "I want to get the grass cut," he said.
We both looked down at the grass—there was a sharp line where my ragged lawn ended and the darker, well-kept expanse of his began. I suspected that he meant my grass.
"There's another little thing," he said uncertainly, and hesitated.
"Would you rather put it off for a few days?" I asked.
"Oh, it isn't about that. At least—" He fumbled with a series of beginnings.
"Why, I thought—why, look here, old sport, you don't make much money, do you?"
"Not very much."
This seemed to reassure him and he continued more confidently.

"I thought you didn't, if you'll pardon my—you see, I carry on a little business on the side, a sort of side line, you understand. And I thought that if you don't make very much—You're selling bonds, aren't you, old sport?"
"Trying to."
"Well, this would interest you. It wouldn't take up much of your time and you might pick up a nice bit of money. It happens to be a rather confidential sort of thing."

I realize now that under different circumstances that conversation might have been one of the crises of my life. But, because the offer was obviously and tactlessly for a service to be rendered, I had no choice except to cut him off there.
"I've got my hands full," I said. "I'm much obliged but I couldn't take on any more work."
He waited a moment longer, hoping I'd begin a conversation, but I was too absorbed to be responsive, so he went unwillingly home.
<citation>Adapted from F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby</citation>

contents.text: Immediately after Nick confirms his willingness to help Gatsby by arranging a meeting with Daisy, Gatsby abruptly changes the subject by offering Nick a job. Gatsby's offer of "a nice bit of money" for little effort is tempting to Nick, but Nick sees it as repayment for a favor, which he finds objectionable. This evidence suggests that the most likely reason that Gatsby offers Nick a job is as repayment for arranging a meeting with Daisy.

has inspired several acclaimed young adult novels, a ballet, and even a Taylor Swift song called "Happiness."
Hollywood studios have adapted the novel for film at least six times.

content.text: The Great Gatsby

pieces.text: screened just a year after the book's publication, at a time when film was still a relatively new medium. It is unknown exactly how the 1926 version went about telling Gatsby's story, as no known copies of that movie exist; it is among the seventy-eight percent of American feature films from the silent era that have been lost to decomposition and neglect.

text.text: His desire to appear casually aloof conflicts with his feelings of excitement for Daisy's visit.

contents.text: These inferences about Gatsby are not supported by the passage:

text.text: His romantic interest in Daisy conflicts with his eagerness to have Nick come to work for him.

content.text: Gatsby does not seem to see a conflict between his interest in Daisy and his interest in keeping Nick close to him.

text.text: His hope that Nick will invite Daisy over conflicts with his fear that Daisy will not remember him.

content.text: Gatsby does not express fear that Daisy has forgotten him.

text.text: His desire for Nick's assistance conflicts with his fundamental disdain for people with Nick's low social standing.

content.text: While it is true that Nick is considerably less wealthy than Gatsby, Gatsby does not act with disdain or intentional disrespect toward his neighbor. If anything,
Gatsby seems deferential to Nick when he says that he doesn't want to put him to any trouble.

contents.text: The details in these quotes suggest that Gatsby is trying to appear casually aloof:

text.text: He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.

content.text: Nick senses that Gatsby wants to talk about Daisy's potential visit but that he is suppressing, or holding back, his desire to broach the subject. A likely explanation for Gatsby's hesitation is that he is trying to project an aura of relaxed confidence.

text.text: "Oh, that's all right," he said carelessly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble."

content.text: Gatsby tries to project a tone of casual indifference about the details surrounding Daisy's visit. While his excessive politeness and his fretting about the lawn suggest that he is actually quite nervous and tense, he seems to want Nick to think that he is very cool and relaxed.

contents.text: The details in this passage suggest that this is why Nick brushes aside Gatsby's job offer:

text.text: Nick is not comfortable accepting a favor in exchange for helping Gatsby.

content.text: Nick says that Gatsby's job offer is obviously in exchange for a service and, as such, he "has no choice" but to reject it. This indicates that Nick does not feel comfortable trading on his connection with Daisy for profit.

contents.text: These inferences are not supported by the passage:

text.text: Nick does not approve of Gatsby's business and can't imagine working with him.

content.text: Nick says that under other circumstances, he would have considered Gatsby's offer seriously. He rejects it because he thinks the offer itself is crass and tactless, not because he disapproves of Gatsby's business practices.

text.text: Nick is offended that Gatsby makes assumptions about Nick's job and finances.

content.text: Nick seems to humbly agree that he doesn't make very much money as a bond salesman. He doesn't seem offended by Gatsby's assumptions.

text.text: Nick's job is keeping him so busy that he doesn't have time to work for Gatsby.

content.text: Nick suggests that he could have been tempted to accept Gatsby's offer if it didn't come with such obvious strings attached. Though he says he can't take on more work, it seems that Nick is using his job as an excuse to reject Gatsby's offer, which he sees as unscrupulous under the circumstances.

Turning a corner, I saw that it was Gatsby's house, lit from tower to cellar.

At first I thought it was another party, a wild rout that had resolved itself into "hide-and-go-seek" or "sardines-in-the-box" with all the house thrown open to the game. But there wasn't a sound. Only wind in the trees, which blew the wires and made the lights go off and on again as if the house had winked into the darkness. As my taxi groaned away I saw Gatsby walking toward me across his lawn.
"Your place looks like the World's Fair," I said.

content.text: Let's go to Coney Island, old sport. In my car."
"It's too late."
"Well, suppose we take a plunge in the swimming pool? I haven't made use of it all summer."
"I've got to go to bed."
"All right."
He waited, looking at me with suppressed eagerness.
"I talked with Miss Baker," I said after a moment. "I'm going to call up Daisy tomorrow and invite her over here to tea."

textContent.text: "Oh, that's all right," he said carelessly. "I don't want to put you to any trouble."
"What day would suit you?"

textContent.text: "How about the day after tomorrow?"
He considered for a moment. Then, with reluctance: "I want to get the grass cut," he said.
We both looked down at the grass—there was a sharp line where my ragged lawn ended and the darker, well-kept expanse of his began. I suspected that he meant my grass.
"There's another little thing," he said uncertainly, and hesitated.
"Would you rather put it off for a few days?" I asked.
"Oh, it isn't about that. At least—" He fumbled with a series of beginnings.
"Why, I thought—why, look here, old sport, you don't make much money, do you?"
"Not very much."
This seemed to reassure him and he continued more confidently.

"I thought you didn't, if you'll pardon my—you see, I carry on a little business on the side, a sort of side line, you understand. And I thought that if you don't make very much—You're selling bonds, aren't you, old sport?"
"Trying to."
"Well, this would interest you. It wouldn't take up much of your time and you might pick up a nice bit of money. It happens to be a rather confidential sort of thing."

I realize now that under different circumstances that conversation might have been one of the crises of my life. But, because the offer was obviously and tactlessly for a service to be rendered, I had no choice except to cut him off there.
"I've got my hands full," I said. "I'm much obliged but I couldn't take on any more work."
He waited a moment longer, hoping I'd begin a conversation, but I was too absorbed to be responsive, so he went unwillingly home.

contents.text: The details in this passage suggest this about Gatsby:

text.text: He is uncomfortable asking Nick for what he really wants.

content.text: When there is a significant lull in the conversation, Nick realizes the reason for Gatsby's visit. Gatsby tries to hide his eagerness about discussing a potential visit from Daisy. This suggests that Gatsby isn't comfortable asking Nick directly for what he wants.

contents.text: The details in this passage do not suggest the following about Gatsby:

text.text: He is desperate to win Nick's friendship.

content.text: Gatsby offers to take Nick to Coney Island, and he asks Nick to go swimming with him, but he does not seem particularly upset when Nick declines these offers.

text.text: He is quietly competitive with Nick about money.

content.text: Gatsby seems uncomfortable throughout this passage. The one thing that seems to offer him some sense of confidence is his wealth relative to Nick's. This suggests that he does not see Nick as a financial competitor.

text.text: He is insincere in his offers to entertain Nick.

content.text: Though he likely has ulterior motives, nothing in the text suggests that Gatsby is being insincere when he invites Nick to Coney Island and to his swimming pool.

contents.text: The details in this passage support this inference about Gatsby's desire to have the grass cut:

text.text: He wants to be sure that Daisy will be impressed when she visits.

content.text: Gatsby brings up the lawn immediately after Nick suggests a day when he might invite Daisy to come over. This suggests that Gatsby wants to have the grass cut in anticipation of Daisy's arrival.

contents.text: These inferences are not supported in the passage:

text.text: He wants to signal his disapproval to Nick regarding the state of Nick's property.

content.text: The appearance of the lawn doesn't seem to concern Gatsby except within the context of Daisy's visit. There is no evidence in the passage to suggest that Gatsby disapproves of the way Nick maintains his property, or that he is trying to signal disapproval to Nick.

text.text: He wants to address the damage to his lawn from the most recent party.

content.text: The passage does not mention damage to the lawn from a party.

text.text: He wants to thank Nick for setting up Daisy's visit by offering him free lawn care.

content.text: Gatsby does mention wanting to have the grass cut, but he seems motivated by a desire to impress Daisy, rather than a desire to show gratitude to Nick.

contents.text: Immediately after Nick confirms his willingness to help Gatsby by arranging a meeting with Daisy, Gatsby abruptly changes the subject by offering Nick a job. Gatsby's offer of "a nice bit of money" for little effort is tempting to Nick, but Nick sees it as repayment for a favor, which he finds objectionable. This evidence suggests that the most likely reason that Gatsby offers Nick a job is as repayment for arranging a meeting with Daisy.

has inspired several acclaimed young adult novels, a ballet, and even a Taylor Swift song called "Happiness."

content.text: The Great Gatsby

pieces.text: screened just a year after the book's publication, at a time when film was still a relatively new medium. We both looked down at the grass—there was a sharp line where my ragged lawn ended and the darker, well-kept expanse of his began. I suspected that he meant my grass.
"There's another little thing," he said uncertainly, and hesitated.
"Would you rather put it off for a few days?" I asked.
"Oh, it isn't about that. At least—" He fumbled with a series of beginnings.
"Why, I thought—why, look here, old sport, you don't make much money, do you?"
"Not very much."
This seemed to reassure him and he continued more confidently.

"I thought you didn't, if you'll pardon my—you see, I carry on a little business on the side, a sort of side line, you understand. And I thought that if you don't make very much—You're selling bonds, aren't you, old sport?"
"Trying to."
"Well, this would interest you. It wouldn't take up much of your time and you might pick up a nice bit of money. It happens to be a rather confidential sort of thing."

I realize now that under different circumstances that conversation might have been one of the crises of my life. But, because the offer was obviously and tactlessly for a service to be rendered, I had no choice except to cut him off there.
"I've got my hands full," I said. "I'm much obliged but I couldn't take on any more work."
He waited a moment longer, hoping I'd begin a conversation, but I was too absorbed to be responsive, so he went unwillingly home.
<citation>Adapted from F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby</citation>
